title: Blossoms, not only in full bloom
translation: Are cherry blossoms only worth seeing in full bloom, and the moon only when the sky is clear? Missing the moon on a rainy night, or staying shut inside and not even noticing spring go by, has its own beauty. The things really worth seeing are branches just about to bloom, and a garden covered in fallen petals. A poem with a note saying "I went to see the blossoms, but they had already fallen" or "Something came up and I couldn't go" is no worse than one headed "Looking at the blossoms". Of course everyone misses the blossoms when they fall and the moon when it goes down. But only someone with no feeling at all says "That branch is finished, and that one. Nothing left to see."

With everything, it's the beginning and the end that are interesting. Love too: is it only about being together? If you really know about love, you've grieved over one that ended before it began. You've brooded over promises that came to nothing, lain awake alone through long nights, thought about someone far away, and remembered the old days in a house gone to weeds.

A full moon shining clear across a thousand miles is fine, but the one you wait up for until nearly dawn is better. It comes up pale and a little blue, through the tops of the cedars deep in the mountains, or slips behind a passing shower for a moment. Nothing is more moving. When its light glitters on the oak leaves as if they were wet, it goes right through you, and you wish you had a friend there who would understand, and you miss the city.
Really, are the moon and the blossoms only for your eyes? You can think about spring without leaving the house, and about the moonlit night from your bed. There's something rich and lovely in that.

People with real taste never look too eager, and they enjoy things casually. It's people from the deep countryside who have to enjoy everything as hard as they can. Under the blossoms they shove and squeeze their way to the front, stare without blinking, drink, make up verses together, and in the end break off big branches without a second thought. They dip their hands and feet in the spring water, they tramp into the snow to leave footprints. They can't just look at anything from a little distance.

I once watched people like that at the Kamo Festival, and it was quite a show. "The procession won't be here for ages, no need to sit in the stand yet." So they sat in a house at the back drinking, eating and playing board games, and left one man in the stand to keep watch. When he called out "Here they come!", they all ran up in a panic, fighting to get to the front, leaning out past the blinds until they nearly fell, pushing each other, not missing a thing, and commenting on everything: "Look at that one! And that!" As soon as it had passed: "Call us for the next one", and down they went. All they care about is the main event, it seems.

The really important people from the city just doze and hardly watch at all. The young ones and the lower staff keep getting up to wait on them, and the attendants standing behind never lean over anyone. Nobody is desperate to see. Leaves of hollyhock hang everywhere, and the whole place looks quietly elegant. Before it's fully light, carriages pull up quietly, you wonder whose each one is, and now and then you recognise someone's driver or servant. Charming ones, dazzling ones, all kinds come and go. It's never boring.

By evening the rows of carriages and all the people packed into every spot have gone who knows where, and soon there's hardly anyone left. Once the crush of carriages is over, the blinds and mats come down, and the place gets lonely right in front of you. That's when you feel how the world works, and it gets to you. If you've watched the street, you've seen the festival.

Among the crowds going back and forth past those stands, I recognised a lot of faces. And it hit me: there aren't that many people in the world after all. Even if I were the last to go, after every one of them, I wouldn't have to wait long. Fill a big jar with water and make a tiny hole in it: even if only a little drips out, if it never stops, it'll be empty soon enough. In a city with this many people, there can't be a day when nobody dies. And it's not just one or two a day. Out at Toribeno, at Funaoka, in the fields and hills, some days there are a lot of funerals, but there's never a day without one. The coffin makers can't keep a single one in stock.

Young or old, strong or weak, it doesn't matter: death comes when you least expect it. That you've made it this far is a small miracle. Can you really relax about the world for even a moment? It's like that counting game with stones, the one called stepchildren: while the stones stand in a row, you don't know which one gets taken. You count, take one, and the rest seem safe. But you keep counting, picking out one here and one there, and in the end none of them gets away.

A soldier going off to war knows death is close, and forgets his home and forgets himself. A man who has turned his back on the world sits in his little hut, quietly playing with his garden stones and water, thinking death is something that happens somewhere else. That's foolish. Even deep in the quiet mountains, won't impermanence come charging in like an enemy army? Facing death there is no different from walking onto a battlefield.

literal: Are blossoms to be seen only in full bloom, and the moon only when it is without shadow?
To long for the moon facing the rain, and, shut indoors, not to know where spring has gone: this too is still moving and deep in feeling.
Treetops about to bloom, gardens with scattered and withered (petals): these are what is most worth seeing.

Even in the headnotes of poems, that they write 'When I went to view the blossoms, they had already fallen' or 'Something got in the way and I did not go': is this inferior to saying 'On seeing the blossoms'?

It is natural to grieve when blossoms fall and the moon sinks, but it is the especially obstinate person who says things like 'This branch and that branch have fallen. Now there is nothing worth seeing.'
In all things, it is the beginning and the end that are interesting.
The love of men and women, too: does it mean only meeting and being together?

To think of the pain of (a love) that ended without meeting, to lament vows that came to nothing, to pass the long night alone till dawn, to think of distant skies, to remember the past at a reed-grown house: this one should call 'loving love'.

Rather than having gazed at the full moon without shadow, out beyond a thousand leagues, (the moon) that one waited for until it rose near dawn is very deep in feeling, bluish in appearance, its light between the trees seen at the cedar tops of deep mountains, the time it hides in a cloud of a passing shower: incomparably moving.
Its glittering on leaves of oak and the like that look wet: that sinks into you, and you think 'if only I had a friend with a heart', and long for the capital.
In general, are moon and blossoms to be seen only with the eyes?
To think of spring without leaving the house, and of the moonlit night while staying in the bedroom: that is very rich in promise and delightful.
A person of quality does not look single-mindedly eager, and the way he enjoys things is casual.
It is the person from the remote countryside who enjoys everything intensely.
Under the blossoms, they twist and push close, stare without looking away, drink sake, compose linked verse, and in the end thoughtlessly break off a big branch.
At a spring they dip their hands and feet, in snow they step down and leave footprints: they see nothing at all from a distance.
The way such people watched the festival was very remarkable.

Saying 'The procession is very late. Until then the stand is not needed', they drank sake and ate in a house at the back, played go, sugoroku and so on, and left a person in the stand; when he said 'They are passing', each ran up competing as if their livers were crushed, leaned out past the blinds almost to the point of falling, pushing one another, watched so as not to miss a single thing, said 'this and that' about everything, and when (the procession) had passed, said 'Until (the next) passes again' and went down.
They probably want only to see the things themselves.
The distinguished people of the capital sleep and do not watch at all.
The young and low-ranking get up and sit down in service, those serving behind people do not lean over unbecomingly, and there is no one who tries unreasonably to see.

In the gracefulness of hollyhock hung everywhere without particular reason, before full daylight, the carriages quietly drawing up are intriguing; when you wonder 'is it this person's or that person's?', there are also ox-drivers, servants and so on that you recognise.
Charming ones and splendid ones come and go in all kinds of ways, and watching it is not boring.

When it grows dark, the carriages that were lined up, and the people who sat packed everywhere: where have they gone? Soon they are few, and when the confusion of carriages is over, the blinds and mats are also taken away, and it becomes lonely before your eyes: that makes you realise the way of the world, and it is moving.

Having watched the avenue: that is having watched the festival; from the fact that among the many people coming and going in front of those stands there were many I recognised, I knew: the number of people in the world is not so very large.
Even if it were fixed that I should die after all these people have passed away, I would surely soon meet (that time).
If you put water in a large vessel and open a narrow hole, even if the dripping is little, if it leaks without pause, it will surely soon run out.
Among the many people in the capital, there cannot be a day when they do not die.
Is it only one or two people in one day?
At Toribeno, Funaoka and other fields and hills, there are days when the number sent off (to their funerals) is large, but there is no day when none is sent.
So those who sell coffins have no time to make them and set them aside.
Not depending on youth, not depending on strength: what comes unexpectedly is the time of death.
That you have escaped until today is a rare wonder.
Can you think of the world as calm even for a moment?

When you make the thing called 'stepchildren standing' with sugoroku stones and set them in a row, you do not know which stone will be taken, but when you count to it and take one, the others seem to have escaped; yet as you count again and again and take out this one and that one, none of them escapes: it is like this.
When a soldier goes out to war, he knows that he is close to death, and forgets his home and forgets himself.
In a grass hut that has turned its back on the world, to quietly amuse oneself with water and stones and think one hears of this (death) as something elsewhere is very foolish.
In the depths of quiet mountains, will the enemy, impermanence, not come rushing?
Facing death there is the same as advancing to the battle line.

notes.quote: 月は隈なきをのみ見るものかは
notes.text: かは: a rhetorical question, 'is it…? (No.)'. One of the most quoted lines in Japanese literature. The whole section answers it, and the answer goes much further than blossoms.

notes.quote: 雨にむかひて月を恋ひ
notes.text: Educated readers would hear quotations here. The 1925 edition points to a poem preface in the Wakan Rōeishū anthology, 'facing the rain, longing for the moon' (對雨戀月; the edition prints the characters in a garbled order), and to a Kokinshū poem: たれこめて{春|はる}のゆくへも{知|し}らぬ{間|ま}に{待|ま}ちし{桜|さくら}もうつろひにけり, 'shut indoors, I did not notice spring passing, and the blossoms I waited for have faded'.

{詞書|ことばがき}: the short prose note before a poem in an anthology, telling when and why it was written. Kenkō's argument is literary: poems about missing the blossoms are not worse than poems about seeing them.
ぞ … める: ぞ needs the attributive form, so めり ('it seems') becomes める. {頑|かたくな}: 'stubborn, insensitive'. Kenkō is rarely polite to people who disagree with him.

notes.quote: 万の事も始め終りこそをかしけれ
notes.text: The thesis in one line, with こそ … けれ. Everything after this extends it: love, the moon, the festival, and finally life itself.
{色|いろ}{好|この}む here means 'to be a true connoisseur of love', not 'to be lecherous'. こそ … め: the realis form of む ('one should call it').
A house overgrown with cogon grass: the classic image of a home where a lover no longer comes. Later, Ueda Akinari used it as the title of a famous ghost story (Ugetsu Monogatari, 1776).
もがな: 'if only there were…'. The perfect moon makes him lonely: he wants someone who would feel it too.

notes.quote: 片田舎の人こそ、色濃くよろづはもて興ずれ
notes.text: こそ … ずれ: the realis form of {興|きよう}ず. {色|いろ}{濃|こ}く: 'thickly, intensely'. This is pure snobbery from the capital, and Kenkō does not hide it.

The festival is the Kamo Festival in the fourth month, today's Aoi Matsuri. The procession went along the main avenue, and nobles had viewing stands ({桟敷|さじき}) built along the route. The hollyhock leaves ({葵|あふひ}) later in the section are its decoration and give the festival its modern name. (In English the festival is called the Hollyhock Festival, but the plant is futaba-aoi, a small wild ginger.)

'As if their livers were crushed': in a panic. The liver ({肝|きも}) is the seat of courage and fear; modern {肝|きも}をつぶす still means 'to be startled'. A small puzzle in the text: やうに needs the attributive form before it, and for つぶる ('to be crushed') that form is つぶるる. The 1925 edition prints つぶる, and the transcription adds a mark (〈＊る〉) that one る is missing. Other editions print つぶるる. This page keeps the text exactly as the 1925 edition has it.
The man left on watch speaks politely to his masters ({候|さうらふ}). It is the only thing he gets to say.

Kenkō's ideal spectator sleeps through the main event. It sounds like a joke, but it is consistent with his thesis: the people of taste come for the whole day, the dawn, the carriages, the evening, not for the highlight.

notes.quote: 大路見たるこそ、祭見たるにてはあれ
notes.text: こそ … あれ: 'THAT is what seeing the festival is'. And then, in the same sentence, the section turns: from the crowd to the faces he recognises, and from there to death.

notes.quote: 大きなる器に水を入れて
notes.text: The leaking vessel: a few drops at a time, and still it empties. A simple image for a city that loses a few people every day.

notes.quote: 柩を鬻ぐもの、作りてうち置くほどなし
notes.text: {鬻|ひさ}ぐ: 'to sell' (a rare kanji). The coffin makers sell everything they make before they can put it down. A grim fact, told completely flat, and that is what makes it so hard to forget.

まま{子|こ}{立|だて}, 'stepchildren standing': a counting game with stones in a circle, where every n-th stone is removed until one is left. It is the Japanese version of what mathematicians call the Josephus problem. It later became a famous puzzle in expanded editions of the arithmetic book Jinkōki (first published 1627), where a stepmother arranges the children so that the stepchildren are removed. Kenkō's point is simpler: you are a stone, and the count reaches everyone.

notes.quote: 無常の敵きほひ来らざらむや
notes.text: や: a rhetorical question, 'will it not…? (It will.)'. The section began with blossoms and ends with impermanence as an army charging into the hermit's quiet mountain.

comments.original: {兼好法師|けんかうほふし}が{徒然草|つれづれぐさ}に、「{花|はな}は{盛|さか}りに、{月|つき}はくまなきをのみ{見|み}るものかは。」とか{言|い}へるは、いかにぞや。……いづこの{歌|うた}にかは、{花|はな}に{風|かぜ}を{待|ま}ち、{月|つき}に{雲|くも}を{願|ねが}ひたるはあらん。さるを、かの{法師|ほふし}が{言|い}へるごとくなるは、{人|ひと}の{心|こころ}にさかひたる、のちの{世|よ}のさかしら{心|ごころ}の、つくりみやびにして、まことのみやび{心|ごころ}にはあらず。
comments.text: "Kenkō writes in Tsurezuregusa: 'Are cherry blossoms only worth seeing in full bloom, and the moon only when the sky is clear?' What is that supposed to mean? … Is there a single poem anywhere that waits for wind to blow on the blossoms, or wishes for clouds over the moon? What that priest says goes against the human heart. It is the too-clever mind of a later age: fake elegance, not true elegance." Norinaga, the great scholar of Japanese classics, answers 470 years later. His argument: the old poems complain about wind and clouds exactly because people long for full blossoms and a clear moon. To grieve over what you missed is honest. To prefer missing it is a pose. In fairness to Kenkō, he never said you should prefer it: he said 'not only' in full bloom.
